We study birational maps with empty base locus defined by almost complete intersection ideals. Birationality is shown to be expressed by the equality of two Chern numbers. We provide a relatively effective method of their calculation in terms of certain Hilbert coefficients. In dimension two the structure of the irreducible ideals leads naturally to the calculation of Sylvester determinants via a computer-assisted method. For degree at most 5 we produce the full set of defining equations of the base ideal. The results answer affirmatively some questions raised by D. Cox.

outputs.L1: We study birational maps with empty base locus defined by almost complete intersection ideals. Birationality is shown to be characterized by the equality of two Chern numbers, and we provide a relatively effective method for computing these numbers in terms of certain Hilbert coefficients. In dimension two, the structure of the irreducible ideals naturally leads to the computation of Sylvester determinants via a computer-assisted method. For degree at most 5, we produce the complete set of defining equations of the base ideal. These results answer affirmatively several questions raised by D. Cox.
outputs.L2: We investigate birational transformations without base points that arise from almost complete intersection ideals. We show that birationality can be characterized by the coincidence of two Chern numbers. We also give a reasonably practical way to compute these numbers using suitable Hilbert coefficients. In the two-dimensional case, the form of the irreducible ideals naturally leads to computing Sylvester determinants with the aid of computer methods. For degrees up to 5, we determine all defining equations of the base ideal. These findings provide positive answers to several questions posed by D. Cox.

The text investigates birational maps whose base locus is empty and which are defined by almost complete intersection ideals. Its main focus is to understand when such maps are birational and how this property can be detected through numerical invariants associated with the ideals involved.

A central result of the work is a characterization of birationality in terms of Chern numbers. Specifically, the authors show that the map is birational precisely when two particular Chern numbers are equal. This provides a numerical criterion for birationality, transforming a geometric question about the map into an algebraic question about invariants of the defining ideal.

The authors also develop an effective method for computing these Chern numbers. Their approach expresses the relevant Chern numbers in terms of certain Hilbert coefficients, making the criterion practical and computable. This is significant because Hilbert coefficients can often be calculated using commutative algebra techniques and computer algebra systems, thereby giving an explicit procedure for testing birationality.

In the special case of dimension two, the paper takes advantage of the structure of irreducible ideals. This additional structure allows the authors to carry out computer-assisted calculations involving Sylvester determinants. These determinants play an important role in obtaining explicit equations and in analyzing the defining relations of the ideals under consideration.

Finally, for maps of degree at most five, the authors go further and produce the complete set of defining equations of the base ideal. This explicit classification not only illustrates the effectiveness of their methods but also answers questions previously raised by D. Cox. Thus, the work combines theoretical criteria, computational techniques, and concrete classifications to advance the study of birational maps defined by almost complete intersection ideals.

The study investigates a class of birational maps defined by almost complete intersection ideals whose base locus is empty. Its main contribution is a criterion for deciding when such a map is birational. This criterion is formulated in terms of the equality of two Chern numbers, which can be computed from Hilbert coefficients associated with the ideals involved. In this way, the problem of testing birationality is translated into an explicit numerical condition, making the criterion effective and suitable for computation.

A central feature of the work is the use of algebraic and homological invariants to connect the geometry of the map with the algebra of its defining ideal. Since the ideals considered are almost complete intersections, they are generated by one more element than a complete intersection, and this structure allows the authors to derive formulas for the relevant Chern numbers. These formulas provide a practical method for determining whether the rational map is in fact birational onto its image, under the assumption that the base locus is empty.

The paper also gives special attention to the two-dimensional case. In this setting, the method becomes particularly explicit and can be implemented with the aid of computer algebra. The authors show how Sylvester determinants arising from the defining data of the map can be calculated computationally. These determinants play an important role in describing the equations of the base ideal and in understanding the implicit structure of the corresponding image.

For maps of degree at most five, the approach is strong enough to produce all defining equations of the base ideal. This gives a complete computational description in these low-degree cases. As a consequence, the work provides affirmative answers to questions posed by D. Cox concerning the explicit determination of such equations and the effectiveness of Sylvester-type methods in this context.

Overall, the study combines techniques from commutative algebra, intersection theory, and computational algebraic geometry. It establishes a numerical birationality test using Chern numbers and Hilbert coefficients, and it demonstrates the practical power of the method in dimension two through explicit computations of Sylvester determinants and defining equations.
outputs.L5:
Birationality, Chern classes, and Hilbert schemes are central concepts in modern algebraic geometry, each offering a different perspective on the structure of algebraic varieties.

**Birationality** studies algebraic varieties up to equivalence on dense open subsets. Two varieties are birational if they have isomorphic function fields, or equivalently, if they are the same outside lower-dimensional subsets. This viewpoint is especially important in classification theory, where one often seeks to understand varieties not by their exact global form, but by their behavior on a large open part. For example, a smooth projective variety may be replaced by a birational model with better geometric properties, such as a minimal model.

**Chern classes** provide characteristic invariants of vector bundles, especially the tangent bundle of a smooth variety. They encode geometric and topological information, such as curvature, intersection numbers, and obstructions to triviality. In algebraic geometry, Chern classes appear in the study of Riemann–Roch theorems, moduli spaces, and enumerative problems. For a smooth projective variety, the Chern classes of its tangent bundle often reflect deep properties of the variety, including positivity, singularity behavior, and deformation theory.

**Hilbert schemes** parametrize families of subschemes of a fixed projective variety with a given Hilbert polynomial. They provide a powerful way to organize geometric objects into moduli spaces. For instance, the Hilbert scheme of points on a smooth surface is itself a smooth variety with rich geometry, closely connected to representation theory, enumerative geometry, and mathematical physics.

These three ideas often interact. Birational transformations can relate different Hilbert schemes or moduli spaces, while Chern classes help compute invariants that remain meaningful across families. In particular, the geometry of Hilbert schemes can be studied through their tangent bundles and associated Chern classes, and birational methods are frequently used to compare different compactifications of moduli spaces. Together, birationality, Chern theory, and Hilbert schemes form a powerful framework for understanding the classification, deformation, and enumeration of algebraic varieties.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main results of a commutative algebra/algebraic geometry paper proving birationality criteria via equality of Chern numbers and computing defining equations of base ideals of degree at most 5.
counterfactuals.output:
The paper’s main contributions can be summarized in two interconnected directions: a birationality criterion expressed through numerical invariants, and explicit computations for low-degree base ideals, especially those arising from plane rational maps/Cremona maps.

## 1. Birationality criteria via equality of Chern numbers

The paper develops criteria for deciding when a rational map is birational onto its image by comparing certain numerical invariants attached to the source, the image, and the base locus.

Roughly, for a rational map

\[
\mathfrak F : X \dashrightarrow Y
\]

defined by a linear system or by homogeneous forms of the same degree, the authors relate birationality to equality of Chern-type numerical data. These invariants measure, in intersection-theoretic terms, how the graph of the rational map differs from the trivial or expected situation.

The main point is that under suitable hypotheses, the map is birational precisely when certain Chern numbers agree. Equivalently, the numerical discrepancy contributed by the base locus vanishes.

In more algebraic language, the criterion compares invariants of the Rees algebra or blowup algebra associated to the base ideal. The graph of the rational map is

\[
\operatorname{Proj} \mathcal R(I),
\]

where \(I\) is the base ideal. Birationality can then be detected by the behavior of this blowup and by numerical data extracted from it.

The result generalizes classical degree formulas for rational maps, where one has expressions of the form

\[
\deg(\mathfrak F)\cdot \deg(Y)
=
\text{a numerical invariant of the defining linear system}
-
\text{contribution from the base locus}.
\]

The paper interprets the base-locus contribution through Chern numbers. When the relevant Chern numbers coincide, the degree of the field extension is forced to be one, hence the map is birational.

Thus, the paper gives an effective numerical test for birationality: instead of explicitly constructing an inverse map, one can verify equality of appropriate Chern numbers.

## 2. Application to base ideals of small degree

A second major part of the paper is computational and classificatory. The authors apply the birationality criteria and Rees-algebra techniques to base ideals generated by forms of degree at most \(5\).

The focus is on ideals defining rational maps, especially plane maps

\[
\mathbb P^2 \dashrightarrow \mathbb P^2
\]

given by triples of homogeneous forms of the same degree. Such ideals are often height-two perfect ideals and are described by Hilbert–Burch matrices. For Cremona maps, the base ideal satisfies strong numerical restrictions coming from the classical Noether equalities.

For degree \(d\leq 5\), the possible base-point multiplicity types are limited, and the paper explicitly analyzes the corresponding ideals.

## 3. Defining equations of the Rees algebra

For each relevant low-degree base ideal, the paper computes or describes the defining equations of the Rees algebra

\[
\mathcal R(I)=R[It].
\]

Equivalently, if

\[
I=(f_1,f_2,f_3)\subset R=k[x,y,z],
\]

one studies the kernel of the natural map

\[
R[T_1,T_2,T_3]\longrightarrow R[It],
\qquad
T_i\mapsto f_i t.
\]

This kernel is the defining ideal of the graph of the rational map.

The paper determines these defining equations for base ideals of degree at most \(5\). Typically, the equations consist of:

1. the linear equations coming from the syzygies of \(I\), i.e. the Hilbert–Burch relations;
2. additional nonlinear equations, often obtained by elimination or Sylvester-type constructions;
3. in favorable cases, enough equations to show that the Rees algebra has the expected form or that the ideal is of fiber type.

A recurring theme is to decide whether the Rees ideal is generated by the symmetric algebra equations together with the equations of the special fiber. In other words, the paper studies when

\[
\mathcal R(I)
\]

is of fiber type.

## 4. Degree-by-degree classification up to degree 5

The authors give an explicit account of the possible base ideals for degrees \(2,3,4,5\), including their syzygy structures and the equations defining their Rees algebras.

For plane Cremona maps, the relevant homaloidal types include, for example,

\[
(2;1^3),
\]

\[
(3;2,1^4),
\]

and higher-degree types such as those occurring in degrees \(4\) and \(5\). For each type, the paper analyzes the possible Hilbert–Burch matrices and derives the defining equations of the associated blowup algebra.

The degree \(\leq 5\) restriction makes the classification manageable while still illustrating the complexity of the general problem.

## 5. Consequences for rational and Cremona maps

The computations have geometric consequences.

They allow one to:

- verify when a given rational plane map is birational;
- describe the graph of the map explicitly;
- compute the implicit equation of the image when the image is a hypersurface;
- understand the exceptional locus and base-point behavior;
- determine whether the base ideal has desirable algebraic properties such as being saturated, perfect, of linear type, or of fiber type.

In the Cremona case, the paper’s results give explicit algebraic models for the graphs of low-degree plane Cremona transformations.

## 6. Overall significance

The paper combines intersection theory, commutative algebra, and explicit computation. Its main achievement is to show that birationality can be detected numerically through equality of Chern numbers, and then to make this criterion concrete by computing the defining equations of Rees algebras for base ideals of degree at most \(5\).

In short, the paper provides:

- a Chern-number criterion for birationality;
- formulas relating degree, base locus contributions, and Chern data;
- explicit Rees-algebra equations for low-degree base ideals;
- a detailed classification/computation for degree \(\leq 5\);
- applications to plane rational maps and Cremona transformations.

counterfactuals.output: Recent work on almost complete intersection ideals defining birational maps has emphasized the interplay between the homological structure of the base ideal and the projective geometry of the induced rational map. In this setting, one studies ideals \(I=(f_0,\ldots,f_n)\subset k[x_0,\ldots,x_n]\) generated by forms of the same degree with \(\operatorname{ht} I=n\), so that \(I\) is one generator away from being a complete intersection and determines a rational map \(\mathbb P^n\dashrightarrow \mathbb P^n\). Birationality can often be detected through the Rees algebra, syzygies, or the Jacobian dual matrix, while the base scheme contributes correction terms to numerical invariants of the map. In dimension \(2\), where the base locus is zero-dimensional, these corrections become especially explicit: the degree formula relates the degree of the plane map, the multiplicities of the base points, and the degree of the inverse map, and effective computations of Chern numbers can be carried out from a locally free resolution of the base ideal. For an almost complete intersection base ideal \(I=(f_0,f_1,f_2)\subset k[x,y,z]\), the Hilbert–Burch matrix gives concrete equations for the base scheme, while the associated Rees ideal provides explicit defining equations for the graph of the birational map. Thus, in the surface case, one obtains a particularly computable picture: the birationality criterion, the Chern-number contributions, and the defining equations of the base locus can all be expressed directly in terms of the syzygy matrix and the degrees of its entries.

In addition, we use Sylvester determinants to obtain effective formulas and criteria for the birationality condition. These computations provide a concrete bridge between the algebraic structure of the base ideal and the geometry of the induced rational map.
